notes.text: The setting of this address is not clear, though it was probably a different occasion than ch. 11. From now on, Samuel will no longer be the judge of all Israel: the age of kingship has begun. But this is neither a retirement ceremony for Samuel nor his last public address; his authority as the prophet who gives the word of God to the king and people of Israel remains powerful (see 12:18), and he has one more king to anoint (ch. 16).

Samuel asks the people to testify to his honorable behavior as a judge, in contrast to that of his sons (see 8:3). Whose ox have I taken? Samuel has not used his office as a means of personal enrichment (see notes on 8:3; 8:14–15).
the Baals and the Ashtaroth. That is, the foreign gods and goddesses; see note on 7:3–4.
No king in Israel is exempt from obeying the Lord’s commandments.
empty things. Worthless idols. Those who trust in them receive only emptiness in return.
Praying and instruction are two of Samuel’s major roles as prophet, even now that Israel has its king.
Both the people and the king are required to obey the Lord.
